openers.water: Water never stays put. It circles endlessly between sky, land and sea, changing form as it goes, and on its way across the land it reshapes the ground. This part of the course follows that water as it flows over the surface, gathers into channels and carries soil away with it. It also looks at ground that sinks beneath people's feet, and at the ponds, channels and plantings people build to keep runoff from doing harm.
openers.erosion-and-sediment: Rain that cannot soak in has to go somewhere. Sometimes it falls faster than the ground can take it; sometimes the soil is already full and every hollow brimming. Either way it spreads across the surface as overland flow, and in towns, roofs and roads speed it on. This chapter starts with that flow and the ways land development changes it. It then turns to the tools people use to tame it, from ponds that hold a storm back to planted channels that clean the water, and even a humble bale of cereal straw.

soil-water-079.title: The water cycle, a sun-driven loop through the soil
soil-water-079.text: Each year about 505,000 cubic kilometers of water fall from the sky, and 398,000 of them land on the oceans. The rest meets the ground. The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between reservoirs on, above and below the Earth's surface, changing form as it goes. Its fluxes are evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, sublimation, infiltration, and flow over and beneath the surface. Energy from the sun powers every one of them. Rain reaching land has two paths. It flows over the ground as {{ref:soil-water-019}}, or it soaks in by {{ref:soil-water-180}} and becomes soil moisture or groundwater. Shallow water may seep back to streams or be drawn up and transpired by plants. Deeper water recharges aquifers, where it can stay for thousands of years. Evapotranspiration is the sum of water transpired by plants and water evaporated from the soil. Not all soil water is alike. A global study of stable water isotopes found that some soil moisture is less available for recharging groundwater or feeding plants. Moving water also remakes the land through weathering, erosion and deposition. Runoff carries almost all the eroded sediment and phosphorus that travel from land to water bodies.

soil-water-019.title: Surface runoff: rain that cannot soak in
soil-water-019.text: A roof sheds every drop that hits it, and so does a parking lot. Surface runoff is the unconfined flow of water over the ground, as opposed to flow in stream channels. It is also called overland flow. It forms when rain, stormwater or meltwater cannot soak in fast enough. Either the soil is saturated, or rain arrives faster than the soil can absorb it. Both are limits on {{ref:soil-water-180}}. Impervious areas such as roofs and pavement are a common cause, since water cannot enter the ground there at all. Soil storage absorbs light showers. On ancient Australian and southern African soils, dense networks of proteoid roots can prevent runoff even in heavy rain. Runoff is a major part of {{ref:soil-water-079}} and the main agent that wears soil away by water. It carries soil particles about 0.001 to 1.0 mm across. The larger ones settle quickly, while the small ones stay suspended over long distances. The land whose runoff drains to a common point is a drainage basin. Runoff also picks up petroleum, pesticides and fertilizers, making it a nonpoint source of pollution, one with no single outlet. Farm runoff drives {{ref:soil-env-019}} downstream, along with {{ref:soil-env-020}}. In towns it is a main cause of urban flooding, from streets under water to damp and mold in basements.

soil-water-081.title: Stormwater and the dirty first flush
soil-water-081.text: In a forest, much of a storm soaks into the soil. In a city, much of it races to the nearest stream. Stormwater is water from precipitation, including heavy rain and meltwater from hail and snow. It may infiltrate and become groundwater, pond in hollows, evaporate or run off as {{ref:soil-water-019}}. Forest plants help the soil absorb it: they improve infiltration, intercept rain and take up water through their roots. Impervious surfaces and compacted soil do the opposite. More water runs off, streams swell, and erosion and flooding follow. Because storms flush the water away, little is left to recharge groundwater or feed streams in dry weather. Most runoff reaches streams untreated, carrying trash, sediment, nutrients, bacteria, pesticides, metals and petroleum byproducts. The first flush of a storm is usually the most concentrated. Phosphorus from fertilizers, or bound to sediment from building sites and farms, feeds algae and toxic cyanobacteria blooms in lakes. Treatment facilities usually rely on Stokes' law to settle particles larger than 40 microns, and they hold water back against downstream flooding.

soil-water-084.title: Subsidence: when the ground itself sinks
soil-water-084.text: In many places, pumping water or oil out of the ground has lowered the surface by as much as 9 meters. Subsidence is the downward movement of the Earth's surface, caused by natural processes or by human activity. It involves little or no sideways motion, which sets it apart from slope movements. Its causes are varied. Groundwater can dissolve carbonate rock. Sediments compact gradually, much as in {{ref:soil-phys-110}}. Mines hollow out the ground, wells draw groundwater or petroleum from it, and tectonic forces warp the crust. The pumping alone has cost hundreds of millions of US dollars. In karst, ground of soluble rock hollowed out by caves, a weakened cave roof can collapse and drop rock and earth into the void. The sinkholes left behind may be many hundreds of meters deep. Even buildings play a part. The weight of high towers can press down the soil beneath them, a problem already felt in New York City, the San Francisco Bay Area and Lagos. Lowered ground raises flood risk, especially on river flood plains and deltas. Where it settles unevenly, buildings tilt or crack.

soil-water-086.title: Runoff, from hillslope to river channel
soil-water-086.text: Water moving across the land changes its name along the way. Runoff is the flow of water across the land, a major part of the water cycle. Before it reaches a watercourse it is surface runoff, or overland flow; once inside one it is streamflow, or channel runoff. Channel flow is fed by hillslope runoff, groundwater flowing out of the ground and discharges from pipes. Hydrologists measure it with stream gauges or estimate it with the Manning equation. A record of flow over time is a hydrograph. When the volume of water exceeds what a channel can hold, the result is a flood.

soil-water-089.title: Straw, the half of the harvest left behind
soil-water-089.text: About half the weight of a cereal crop is not grain at all. Straw is the dry stalks of cereals such as barley, oats, rice, rye and wheat, left after the grain and chaff are removed. It has a second life protecting soil. It makes an excellent mulch, covers the ground after wildfires and is built into small dams across streams. Straw bales are sometimes set out to control sediment on construction sites, but they often protect water quality poorly and need much upkeep. The US EPA prefers {{ref:soil-water-093}}, {{ref:soil-water-098}} or {{ref:soil-water-254}}. Mixed with clay-rich subsoil and water, straw also binds cob and adobe, two earth building materials.

soil-water-090.title: Retention basins, ponds that hold back the storm
soil-water-090.text: City pavement rushes rain into the drains; a retention basin slows it down. It is an artificial pond with a permanent pool of water and plants around its edge, built to manage {{ref:soil-water-081}}. The pond contains the surge and releases it slowly, reducing flooding downstream. It also traps suspended sediment, often abundant in runoff from construction and road sanding, while its plants take up dissolved nutrients. It can stand in for the absorption of a forest lost to development. A detention basin, or dry pond, holds water only for a while. An infiltration basin sends stormwater down to groundwater through permeable soil.

soil-water-091.title: Land development and the soil it seals away
soil-water-091.text: Soil under a road or a building is, in effect, used up. Land development is the alteration of a landscape, such as turning natural land over to farming or housing, or dividing it into building lots. Construction brings roads, scraped topsoil, compaction, chemical change from stabilizing the soil, impervious surfaces and polluted runoff. It seals the soil off from rainfall and the nutrient cycle, leaving it infertile. New farmland usually comes from forest, savanna or grassland cleared by assarting, the grubbing up of woodland, or by slash-and-burn. Reclaiming wasteland or sealed ground is rarer, for lack of fertile soil. Profitable improvement can still degrade land, through salt buildup from saline irrigation water or erosion after drainage.

soil-water-092.title: Bioswales, planted channels that clean runoff
soil-water-092.text: A bioswale is a channel that gathers and carries stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution from it. It is planted, mulched or xeriscaped, meaning landscaped with dry-climate plants, and has gently sloping sides of less than 6%. It is built on soil with no more than 5% clay. The design keeps water in the swale as long as is safe. Plants catch pollutants and let them settle, and they then decompose or are broken down by soil bacteria. A bioswale slows runoff, recharges groundwater and reduces flooding and erosion. It suits places with much impervious surface that must handle a storm's first flush. In {{ref:soil-env-218}}, swales harvest water.

soil-water-020.title: When rain outruns the soil: Hortonian flow
soil-water-020.text: Rain can run off even a soil that is far from full. Infiltration-excess overland flow is runoff that forms when rain falls faster than the ground can absorb it and the surface hollows are already full. It is also called Hortonian overland flow, after Robert E. Horton, or unsaturated overland flow. It is commonest in arid and semi-arid regions with intense rain and sealed soil surfaces. It is also common in towns, where pavement blocks infiltration. It differs from {{ref:soil-water-021}}, which begins only once the soil itself is saturated.

soil-water-024.title: Four ways to limit the damage runoff does
soil-water-024.text: Runoff mitigation covers the measures that limit the harm done by surface runoff. They fall into four groups. Land-use codes encourage narrow sidewalks and pavers set in earth, so that as much water as possible soaks into town ground. Controls on erosion and sediment have been required of builders by some governments since the 1960s, among them straw bales, {{ref:soil-water-093}} and limits on bare graded ground. Flood control uses holding ponds, or detention basins, to buffer peak flows, and energy dissipators to slow water in channels. Chemical controls include double containment of underground tanks, fewer approved pesticides and stricter rules for fertilizers and weedkillers.

soil-water-021.title: When the soil is already full: Dunne runoff
soil-water-021.text: Soil that is already soaked cannot take in more rain. Saturation-excess overland flow is runoff produced at once when rain keeps falling on saturated soil whose surface hollows are full. It is also called saturated overland flow or Dunne runoff. Its timing depends on the {{ref:soil-water-155}} left from earlier rain, known as antecedent soil moisture. The wetter the soil starts, the sooner runoff begins. Because saturated soil absorbs less rain, the same volume of rainfall produces more runoff and more erosion.

soil-water-022.title: Throughflow, water that slips back out of the hillside
soil-water-022.text: Not all runoff travels on the surface. Subsurface return flow, also called throughflow, is water that soaks into a hillside upslope, moves sideways through the soil and seeps back out near a channel. Along the way the flow shrinks. Some water returns to the air by evapotranspiration, some is held in small surface hollows and some infiltrates. Whatever remains ends up in a river, lake, estuary or ocean.

soil-water-023.title: Urban runoff, from rooftops to storm drains
soil-water-023.text: In a city, rain lands mostly on surfaces that shed it. Urban runoff is surface runoff from rain, landscape irrigation and car washing, created by urbanization. Roads, parking lots, sidewalks and roofs send polluted stormwater to storm drains instead of letting it percolate through soil. Less water reaches the ground below, so the water table falls and droughts grow worse. More water stays on the surface, so flooding grows worse too. Most municipal storm sewers discharge the water untreated into streams, rivers and bays. There, erosion and siltation can become major problems.

soil-water-080.title: How clearing and building rewire the local water cycle
soil-water-080.text: Change the land cover and the water moves differently. Land use and the water cycle names the local and regional changes to the water cycle that follow changes in land use and land cover. Urbanization, farm expansion and deforestation can increase {{ref:soil-phys-082}} and impervious cover. Both lower the soil's infiltration capacity and raise surface runoff. Locally, clearing forest reduces soil moisture, evaporation, rainfall and snowfall. City pipes cut both ways. Stormwater drains lower runoff rates and raise groundwater recharge, while leaking sewers add recharge but can contaminate groundwater.

soil-water-082.title: Managing stormwater for quantity and quality
soil-water-082.text: A street sweeper and a planted swale belong to the same toolkit. Stormwater management is the control of both the quantity and the quality of stormwater. Its best management practices range from engineered devices, such as {{ref:soil-water-090}}, to routine chores such as street sweeping. Its technical aims include controlling flooding and erosion. Engineers build retention basins, filter vaults and vortex separators that remove coarse solids. Nature-based options, such as ponds, swales and {{ref:soil-water-260}}, work alongside pipes and concrete channels and can also give wildlife habitat. Passive treatment lets gravity carry water through ditches and pipes, with gel flocculants, jute fiber filters and silt retention mats to settle the sediment.

soil-water-083.title: How city stormwater opens sinkholes in karst
soil-water-083.text: Undisturbed karst keeps a quiet balance with the rain. Soil and rock fragments choke the openings in the rock and limit their growth, and the drainage keeps pace with most storms. Cities upset that balance. Urban karst areas lack surface streams, so extra runoff from roofs and streets moves down through the ground. Once the flow can carry soil and rock, the openings grow fast. The result is a stormwater sinkhole, a collapse caused when urban stormwater drains through karst and carries soil and rock fragments away, a sudden form of {{ref:soil-water-084}}. Under a roof of competent limestone there is often no surface warning before an opening collapses. Planners are advised to avoid karst for new development.

soil-water-087.title: Turning a rainstorm into a predicted flood curve
soil-water-087.text: Hydrologists need to know how much water a storm will send downstream, and when. A rainfall-runoff model describes how rainfall on a drainage basin is converted into {{ref:soil-water-086}}. It takes a rainfall event, entered as a hyetograph, a record of rainfall over time, and turns it into a surface runoff hydrograph. Every such model must be calibrated before use. The linear reservoir model is well known but of limited use. A non-linear reservoir applies more widely, but only where rain falls roughly evenly over the catchment. Large study areas are split into sub-catchments, whose hydrographs are combined by flood routing.

soil-water-085.title: Ground that sinks and rises with the seasons
soil-water-085.text: A felled tree can make the ground rise for up to 25 years. Seasonal subsidence and heave is the sinking of the ground as clay-rich soils dry and shrink with the seasons, and its rise again when they rewet. Clay's very small particles make such soils sensitive to changes in moisture, the behavior described in {{ref:soil-phys-028}}. Foundations above the depth reached by seasonal drying move with the soil, which can crack buildings with tapering cracks. Growing trees dry the soil cumulatively. When a tree declines or is felled, that deficit reverses, and the soil heaves, rising and spreading.

soil-water-107.title: Models that follow water and everything it carries
soil-water-107.text: Hydrological transport models came into use in the 1960s and 1970s, when environmental laws demanded water-quality forecasts and computing power became widely available. Such a model simulates the flow of rivers, streams, groundwater or drainage fronts and calculates water quality. Physically based versions represent surface runoff, subsurface flow, evapotranspiration and channel flow. Stochastic versions link inputs such as rainfall to outputs such as runoff statistically. Their surface runoff element lets them assess sediment, fertilizer, pesticides and other chemical contaminants. The groundwork came from Robert E. Horton's work on surface runoff, joined to quantitative treatment of erosion.

soil-water-073.title: The ion cloud that decides whether clay holds together
soil-water-073.text: Salt can decide whether a clay stands firm. Clay platelets carry permanent and pH-dependent negative charges, as {{ref:soil-chem-079}} describes, balanced by cations such as Na+ on their surfaces, in interlayers or in the pore water. The electrical double layer is that cloud of balancing cations around each platelet, and its thickness depends on the water's salinity. In salty water the layer is compressed, so the platelets flocculate into stable aggregates. When rain leaches salt out of uplifted marine clay, the layer expands. Stronger repulsion then disperses the platelets, called peptization, and the clay is destabilized. Adding salt back compresses the layer again, and {{ref:soil-water-071}} rapidly regains its strength.

soil-water-255.title: Four letters that rank soils by runoff
soil-water-255.text: The NRCS sorts soils into four hydrologic soil groups, A to D, by how readily they take in water. The group is used to choose a {{ref:soil-water-088}}. Group A, mostly deep, well-drained sands and gravels, has a final infiltration rate above 7.6 mm (0.30 in) per hour and low runoff potential. Group B takes in 3.8 to 7.6 mm per hour. Group C, often with an impeding layer or fine texture, manages 1.3 to 3.8 mm. Group D has high runoff potential. It covers swelling clays, soils with a permanent high water table or a claypan near the surface, and shallow soils over impervious material. The group is picked from measured infiltration rates, a survey such as the NRCS Web Soil Survey, or a soil professional's judgment.

soil-water-088.title: The curve number, one figure for a storm's runoff
soil-water-088.text: A single number between 30 and 100 can estimate how much of a storm will run off the land. That number is the runoff curve number, CN, an empirical value used in hydrology to predict direct runoff or infiltration from rainfall excess. The US Department of Agriculture developed it, through the agency now called the {{ref:soil-hist-050}}, from runoff measured on small catchments and hillslope plots. A curve number depends on the area's {{ref:soil-water-255}}, land use, treatment and hydrologic condition. Lower numbers mean more permeable soil and low runoff potential; higher numbers mean more runoff. No runoff starts until the initial abstraction, such as infiltration and interception, is met. That threshold was long taken as 0.2 S, but 0.05 S may suit urban watersheds better. Curve numbers are adjusted for antecedent moisture: dry (AMC I), average (AMC II) and moist (AMC III). The method works storm by storm and should not be applied to a single annual rainfall total. Even so, it is widely used as an efficient way to estimate approximate direct runoff.
